challenges.name: inject-the-clock-quiz
challenges.title: Whose clock is the test reading?
challenges.description: Two tests from the deadline incident: one freezes the system time with Vitest and reads the day of the month, the other passes a clock to submissionStatus but builds that clock from the real time.

questions.explanation: False. vi.setSystemTime freezes an instant: 2026-11-01T06:30:00+07:00 is 2026-10-31T23:30:00Z everywhere. getDate() then converts that instant to the local time zone of the process running the test, so the laptop in UTC+7 gets 1 (1 November, 06:30) and the UTC runner gets 31 (31 October, 23:30). The misconception is that a fake clock makes all date arithmetic deterministic; it fixes the instant, not the time zone. Use getUTCDate() with an explicit offset, or Intl.DateTimeFormat with a timeZone option, and run the suite with TZ=UTC as well as your local zone.

True. The function no longer reads the real clock, but the test does: it builds both now and the deadline from new Date(). At 01:30 on 28 October in Vietnam the instant is 2026-10-27T18:30Z, so today is "2026-10-27" and the deadline is 27 October 23:59 in UTC+7 (16:59Z), more than the 15-minute grace in the past: the function correctly answers closed. The misconception is that injecting a clock makes a test deterministic by itself. It only helps when the test passes a fixed instant, for example { now: () => new Date("2026-10-31T16:59:00Z") } with a fixed deadline.

challenges.name: submission-deadline-with-clock
challenges.title: A deadline function that takes a clock
challenges.description: CodeDev decides whether a learner may still submit an assignment. The shipped submissionStatus read new Date() inside, so its test built "today" from the real clock and failed every night between 00:00 and 07:00 Vietnam time. Write submissionStatus(assignment, clock) so that it reads the current time only from clock.now() (never new Date() or Date.now()). assignment.deadline is a wall-clock time "YYYY-MM-DDTHH:mm" in the learner's fixed UTC offset assignment.utcOffsetMinutes (420 = UTC+7, 0 = UTC, -300 = UTC-5, an integer between -720 and 840); the deadline instant is that wall time at second 0 in that offset, so "2026-10-31T23:59" at 420 is 2026-10-31T16:59:00.000Z. Return "on-time" when now <= deadline, "late" when deadline < now <= deadline + graceMinutes, "closed" when now is later than that, and "invalid" when the deadline does not match YYYY-MM-DDTHH:mm exactly, is not a real date and time (2026-02-29T10:00, 2026-10-31T24:00, minute 60, month 13), or graceMinutes is not a whole number >= 0. Input (read by the runner): a JSON list of { assignment: { id, deadline, utcOffsetMinutes, graceMinutes }, at: [ISO instants] }. For every instant the runner builds a clock fixed at it and prints "<id> at <instant>: <status>", one line per instant.
hints: If you had to compare two numbers to decide on-time, late or closed, which two numbers would they be, and in which unit? Where does each one come from?

Look at Date.UTC(year, monthIndex, day, hours, minutes): it reads its arguments as UTC and returns milliseconds. The wall time is in the learner's offset, so the real instant is earlier than that UTC reading for a positive offset. For the invalid cases, check what Date.UTC does with day 30 of February, and compare the fields of the result with what you parsed.

A similar example on other values: a live session at "2027-01-05T09:00" in UTC-5 (offset -300) starts at Date.UTC(2027, 0, 5, 9, 0) - (-300) * 60000, which is 2027-01-05T14:00:00.000Z. With 10 minutes of grace, a clock at 14:10:00.000Z is still inside the grace period and one at 14:10:00.001Z is not.
